readings.alternative: DNA's authority rests on durable reviewable records; the comparison redistributes who can later question an analysis rather than replacing subjective judgment with objectivity.
Narcotics kept crystal tests because statutory turnaround and only two instruments left no other way to clear its caseload; values and a sheltered debate are secondary.
Forensic biology is not a fixed benchmark above the others but one more judgment-laden, reviewed unit whose method was itself evaluated in court and by the Academy first.
Units differ by the kind of change offered: all took on record-adding changes and none judgment-replacing ones, so firearms had already changed by adding images.
The comparison's edge may run between the three units, with toxicology outside it, its change tracing to accreditation and courtroom strategy linked to DNA only by the author.
The narcotics outcome is a provisional snapshot at fieldwork's end: nothing had yet been required, holding on reflected capacity, and change was anticipated.
Whether analysts expected personal challenge in the local court alone explains all three outcomes; values only describe how units talked about decisions exposure had already made.
The narcotics dispute is a power contest within the occupation over whose regional methods become compulsory, with access to standard-setting authority deciding the stakes.
Unit values partly reflect self-selection and transfers, analysts disliking repetitive instrument work moving into narcotics, rather than values learned through doing the work.
Toxicology and firearms differ in whether an accreditor-scheduled plan already existed; the court case's nearness set the date of change, not whether change happened.
Distinct unit cultures partly result from hiring, transfers and self-sorting of analysts into preferred work, not only from values the work itself instils.
Responses are moves to protect unit standing and irreplaceability against a director treating analysts as interchangeable; status and power, not the work's nature, drive them.
Narcotics and toxicology differed in how much routine work the change would displace and its cost in instruments, time and caseload, not in fit with values.
Only firearms met a comparison with DNA; toxicology and narcotics met other demands, uncertainty figures or reviewable output, tied to DNA only by the author.
A standing accreditation requirement and existing plan, absent for firearms, made toxicology change; the immediate court route only determined when the change happened.
Narcotics defended a workable production system under legal deadlines and limited equipment; toxicology's change added calculations while narcotics' would replace its main route.
DNA's authority rests on making judgments available for later inspection; the units' disputes concern how far their work can be reopened by reviewers and courts.
Narcotics resisted because two instruments and long runs could not process its caseload under turnaround rules; knowing GC/MS is not capacity to use it at scale.
Each unit took up the reachable DNA feature, a reviewable record; firearms had already changed to image-backed, countersigned documentation, refusing only numbers.
Unit values record who came, stayed and left; narcotics' dislike of standardised work was brought by members leaving toxicology, so responses track membership.
Firearms had already adopted DNA's reviewable-record element through countersigned image documentation, refusing only statistics; units differ in which piece of the model each could take.
Toxicology's change was a pre-existing accreditation project brought forward by litigation; the DNA comparison at most altered the timetable, not the change's content or adoption.
Toxicology's change was a planned accreditation step brought forward by a DUI defence tactic, not a response to DNA profiling.
Toxicology's change was ongoing ISO accreditation work accelerated by one court date; it is ordinary standards compliance, not a spillover from DNA.
All units follow one rule: revise work when a credible local challenge makes continuing costly, otherwise defend it; exposure decides, values only shape the form.
Responses track what change would cost each unit in instruments, staff time and deadlines; values are only the language in which those costs were expressed.
Occupational values are partly the residue of sorting within one lab, placement by vacancy and exit by preference, so forced change could also produce transfer requests.
Toxicology completed an existing accreditation project early because a court challenge made it urgent; DNA was a persuasive comparison, not the determinant of the reform.
